tagline.text: A windswept ridge trek on Mount Mariveles

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Day hike or 2 days and 1 night

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,200~1,600 (day hike from Manila by public transport, per person)

children.text: Tarak Ridge is a ridge on Mount Mariveles (roughly

class) at the tip of the Bataan Peninsula, and it is a popular hike close to Manila. You start from the village of Alas-asin, pass the Papaya River, climb to the ridge, and look out over Manila Bay and the South China Sea.

Tarak Ridge is a ridge on one side of Mount Mariveles, at the southern end of the Bataan Peninsula on Luzon. Mount Mariveles is a volcanic massif at the southern end of the Zambales Mountains, and English Wikipedia's text and volcano databases give its peak height as about
. Tarak Ridge is the best-known hiking destination on the mountain, and the jump-off point is Barangay Alas-asin in Mariveles.
Hiking guides list the ridge itself at about
above sea level and Tarak Peak at the end of the ridge at about

. It is often rated about 4 out of 9 as a "major climb" and classed as trail class 3. There are no technical rock sections, but the uphill is long and some stretches require grabbing roots and branches, so it suits people who have done one or two easier mountains rather than complete beginners.

The route has three main parts: an exposed walk along grassland trails from Alas-asin, the Papaya River where you can get water, and the steep forest climb that ends at the ridge. On a clear day the ridge opens up views toward the Bataan Peninsula and the South China Sea, and it is famous for the sky turning red at dusk. The wind on the ridge is very strong, so many people pitch a tent and sleep there. The route up to the ridge is an out-and-back on one line, so getting lost is relatively unlikely, but some hikers report confusing forks in the forest, and many guides recommend going with a guide.

It is a 3–4 hour bus ride from Manila, so hiking clubs and group tours crowd the trail every weekend. Korean hiking groups also enjoy both the pre-dawn day hike and the overnight camping hike. Rules and fees change often, so check the latest notice at the Alas-asin barangay office before you go. Decide your schedule first. A day hike starts before dawn and means walking all day, so it is tiring, while the overnight trip means more gear but a more relaxed pace. If this is your first time, joining a group tour or a hiking club schedule that handles transport, registration, and a guide in one package is a common choice; in that case, always check what is included and whether meals are covered.

blocks.title: Sunset and sunrise from the ridge

children.text: From the camping spot on the ridge you can watch the sky turn red at dusk and the sunrise in the early morning. When the weather is clear, the view opens all the way to the horizon over the South China Sea.

The Papaya River, which you reach after walking for a few hours from the start, is almost the only place to refill water on the hike. There is no water at the ridge campsite, so fill up enough here before climbing. Many hikers also boil the water or filter it once more before drinking.
About
30 minutes
further up from the ridge is Tarak Peak, at about
above sea level. People who want a wider view than the ridge gives go up before sunset or the next morning.

Above the Papaya River, the trail runs through forest tangled with roots and vines. It is deeply shaded and cool, a contrast to the heat of the grassland section below. Some stretches require pulling yourself up by roots and branches, so gloves are handy.
Hiking reports recommend sleeping one night and coming down the next day more than any other plan. You can see both sunset and sunrise from the ridge, and it is less tiring than a day hike.

blocks.title: Starting point for Mount Mariveles traverses

children.text: Tarak Ridge is sometimes described as part of a longer traverse that links to other peaks on Mount Mariveles. You can try it once you are used to longer hikes, but the route is complicated to follow without a guide.

items.title: Day hike
items.subtitle: Pre-dawn start, back in the evening

children.text: Leave Manila. For a group tour, meeting around midnight and traveling by van is common.
Arrive at the Alas-asin barangay office, register, and be assigned a guide. You can eat breakfast at a small shop nearby.
Start trekking. You either walk or take a tricycle for about
1.5km
to the area near Nanay Cording's house.
Arrive at the Papaya River and rest. This is the last place to refill water.
Climb to Tarak Ridge, take photos, and rest.
If you like, go on to Tarak Peak and back.
Start the descent. Many people get hurt going down, so take it slowly.
Return to the jump-off, wash up, and take transport back to Manila. Check the last bus time in advance.
These times are an example from one hiking guide and vary with your pace, the weather, and traffic.
Travel from Manila by bus and arrive at the village of Alas-asin.
Register at the barangay office and arrange a guide.
Start trekking.
Have lunch at the Papaya River and refill your water.
Arrive at the ridge and pitch your tent in a spot sheltered from the wind.
Watch the sunset and have dinner.
Watch the sunrise, have breakfast, and pack up.
Start the descent, passing the Papaya River on the way down to the jump-off.
There is no water on the ridge, so carry up from the Papaya River all the water you will need until the next morning.
From Manila (Cubao, Pasay, and elsewhere), take a bus bound for Mariveles and get off at Barangay Alas-asin. The trip usually takes
3–4 hours
Genesis and Bataan Transit buses run toward Bataan.
You can also take a bus to Balanga and transfer to a minibus to Alas-asin.

items.title: By car or van from Manila

children.text: Take NLEX and SCTEX, exit at Dinalupihan, and follow the Roman Highway toward Balanga and Mariveles.
Parking near the jump-off is limited, so it is best to arrive early.
Group tours are sold as packages with a round-trip van from Manila and registration and a guide included.

items.title: From the village to the jump-off

children.text: Register first at the Alas-asin barangay office, then walk or take a tricycle to the jump-off.
One source lists the tricycle fare at about
per person.
Hiking guides recommend the dry season from November to April. December to February is relatively cool and comfortable for walking.

In March and April the lower grassland section is very hot and brush fires from slash-and-burn farming can occur, so check current conditions. In the rainy season the trail is slippery and camping on the ridge is dangerous.

On weekends and holidays the ridge and jump-off get crowded, and some reports mention lines forming early in the morning on peak weekends. For a quieter trip, consider a weekday hike. Check the weather forecast first, then decide your schedule.

You can find places to stay before or after the hike in Mariveles town or Balanga city. Most people do a day hike or camp on the ridge, so they travel without separate lodging. Room rates vary by season, so check booking apps.

You can have breakfast at small shops near the Alas-asin barangay office, but there are no shops up on the mountain. Bring your own food and emergency rations. After the hike, many people eat in Mariveles or toward Orion.

If you are not going straight back to Manila after the hike, you can plan a night in Balanga city and visit other Bataan sights. Showers and simple washing are available for a fee at facilities near the jump-off.
Register at the barangay office and arrange a guide before you start. Recent sources say a guide is required, so check the latest notice.
Refill water at the Papaya River and carry at least 2–3 liters. A filter or purification tablets make a good backup.
If you camp, pitch your tent by the trees where you are sheltered from the wind, not in the middle of the ridge. The wind is strong, so bring extra tent pegs.
Trekking poles help to protect your knees on the descent.
The ridge is cool and very windy, so bring a windbreaker and warm layers.
Hikers report many rats, so keep your food sealed.
Do not use soap or detergent in the Papaya River. Villages downstream use that water.
Carry all your trash back out.
Many reports say mobile signal is available along most of the trail, but it may vary by area. Get the barangay office's emergency contact number in advance.
Bring a flashlight or headlamp, first-aid supplies, and spare socks. The temperature swing is large, so on the ridge you will feel the difference between midday and night.
The ridge is very windy, the trail can be slippery, and accidents are frequent on the descent, so move slowly and hike with a guide.
The whole section before the Papaya River has little shade and is very hot at midday. Prepare a hat and plenty of water.
There are many roots, clay, and vines, so the trail is slippery when it rains. Wear hiking shoes.
Hikers report seeing venomous snakes (pit vipers) in the forest section. Be careful not to put your hands into the undergrowth.
In March and April, brush fires from slash-and-burn farming can occur. Check the latest notice.
Get back to the jump-off before sunset at the latest so you do not miss the last bus.
Aluminum tent poles are recommended; hikers report that fiberglass poles snapped in the wind on the ridge.
This historic island is about
15–20 minutes
by boat from Mariveles, and you can plan it together if you stay one more day after the hike.
This giant cross memorial inside Bataan is worth a stop if you are interested in war history.
The central city of Bataan, a good place to transfer to a bus bound for Manila or to have a meal.
A beach in Mariveles mentioned in hiking reports as a place to rest after the hike. Check its current condition locally.
